The fatal accident inquiry found that Captain David Traill ignored five low fuel warnings, causing the engines to flame out due to fuel starvation.
The sheriff said the pilot made a conscious decision to ignore the warnings, with fatal consequences.
The sheriff noted the accident would not have occurred if the pilot had followed standard procedure for low fuel warnings.
The sheriff criticized the delay in holding the inquiry and said the Crown Office's investigation team was under-resourced.
Ian O'Prey, father of a victim, expressed anger, saying Capt Traill was made a 'fall guy.'
Clutha owner Alan Crossan expressed shock and disappointment at the report's harshness toward the pilot.
The Crown Office acknowledged the delay was longer than desirable and said improvements were being made.
Airbus Helicopters said it was deeply saddened and committed to safety.

1-16325-6-t.subevent: The reporter met three generations of women survivors of a machete attack: Jesinne Dhewedza lost four fingers, Irene Mave lost her right arm, and Marie Dz'dza lost both hands and a child.
A wave of violence in Djugu territory, starting in December and peaking in February-March, involved attacks on about 120 villages by Lendu men, driving out the Hema ethnic group.
Hadji Ruhingwa Bamaraki, president of the Hema cultural association, said the ethnic cleansing may be genocide.
Over 350,000 people were displaced, with more than 50,000 fleeing to Uganda.
The attacks were largely ignored internationally, exacerbated by a 2017 U.S. policy change affecting peacekeeping.
In the attack on Logo Takpa, the three women were caught by Lendu men they knew and were attacked with machetes.
After the attack, the women walked for days to reach the Mudzi Maria Health Center for treatment.
Refugees crossing Lake Albert to Uganda faced dangers; on February 11, four refugees drowned attempting the crossing.
A cholera outbreak began on February 15, leading to over 2,000 cases; overcrowding and malnutrition at camps worsened, as seen with two orphans at Maratatu settlement.

19-wiki-img/28866-1/28866-1-1.subevent: Disneyland Paris reopens on Thursday at 8:30 AM after seven months of forced closure during the second wave.
The park used the extra week to refine its public welcome with a stricter health protocol than last year's reopening.
Masks remain mandatory for visitors aged 6 and over throughout the park, including queues, shops, hotels, restaurants, and ride cars.
No health pass is required to enter, but visitors are encouraged to self-test before coming.
The park's capacity is halved to a maximum of 28,000 visitors, down from the usual 50,000 per day.
Hugs with characters like Mickey and Pluto are banned until further notice, but selfies are still possible with new photo stands.
Disneyland Paris offers a special cancellation policy: tickets can be cancelled up to three days before the date, and hotel reservations up to seven days before arrival.
During the closure, the park completed installation of two new attractions, Star Wars Legends and Cars Road Trip, and refurbished others like Snow White and Pinocchio.
Gardeners restored the entire irrigation system and replaced the park's 800,000 flowers.

1-16056-7-t.subevent: Colombia's migration agency announced the closure of land and river borders until June 1 to curb the spread of coronavirus.
Director general Juan Francisco Espinosa said they cannot lower their guard and must follow health recommendations to overcome the pandemic.
The borders were expected to reopen on March 1, but exceptions to the closure include freight transport, health emergencies, and other unforeseen emergencies.
Air travel will not be affected by the border closure rules.
The government extended its health state of emergency until at least May 31.
Colombia closed its borders in March last year and was due to open on Saturday, and it is the top destination for Venezuelan migrants.
More than 1.7 million Venezuelans are currently in Colombia.
Colombia has reported more than 2.2 million coronavirus cases and 59,518 deaths.

21-31051-7-t.subevent: Fethi Nourine and his coach Amar Benikhlef gave statements to media announcing their withdrawal from the Tokyo 2020 Olympic judo competition to avoid meeting an Israeli athlete.
The IJF Executive Committee formed an investigative commission to look into the matter.
The investigative commission confirmed the facts, leading to a temporary suspension of Nourine and Benikhlef and assignment of the case to the IJF Disciplinary Commission.
The IJF launched an investigation and notified the Algerian Olympic Committee and the International Olympic Committee.
The Algerian Olympic Committee withdrew the accreditations of the athlete and coach and planned to send them home, applying sanctions.
The IJF stated that the actions were based on the recorded declarations which are in total opposition to its philosophy of non-discrimination and solidarity.
The IJF announced that Nourine and Benikhlef are suspended and will face a decision by the Disciplinary Commission and disciplinary sanctions by the National Olympic Committee of Algeria.

0-4374-2-t.subevent: A small plane crashed just outside Capital Region International Airport just before 9 a.m.
The plane had flown from Indianapolis to Lansing, carrying two pilots and four passengers.
Three people died and three others were critically injured in the crash.
One of the critically injured was later upgraded to stable condition.
Officials said the passengers did not appear to be related.
Officials are waiting to notify next of kin before releasing the identities of the deceased.
The plane was relatively intact despite a hard landing, and there was no fire.
The FAA is sending staff to investigate, and the NTSB has been notified.
Roads near the airport are closed; initial reports indicated people walking around the crash; the cause is unknown.

21-29910-8-1.subevent: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin announced the waiver of self-isolation rules, travel permits, and walking schedules starting June 9, allowing all residents to freely travel and visit public places.

The first phase of reopening included hairdressing salons, veterinary clinics, recruitment agencies, NGOs, cemeteries, car sharing services, film and sound recording studios, research centers, and theaters, concert halls, and circuses for rehearsals.
Starting June 16, dentist clinics, real estate, leasing, law, accounting, consulting, advertising, and market research firms resumed, and sports competitions could be held with ≤10% occupancy.
Also starting June 16, summer cafes, libraries, museums, exhibition halls, and zoos reopened with visitor limits.
Starting June 23, gyms, fitness clubs, swimming pools, restaurants, cafes, bars, canteens, other public catering outlets, spa salons, sunrooms, steam baths, and saunas were allowed to open.
All reopening organizations must comply with supervisory authorities and Rospotrebnadzor; a decision on the remaining restrictions was deferred.
Sobyanin warned that residents must adhere to self-protection rules including facemasks and social distancing, as the risk of infection remains.
The dates for lifting restrictions may be changed depending on the epidemiological situation.
Moscow reported 2,001 new coronavirus cases, bringing the total to 197,018, with 1,633 recoveries and 51 deaths (the lowest in two weeks), for a total of 2,970 deaths.

Moscow had declared a high alert on March 29, with self-isolation and closures, but began easing on May 12 (construction) and June 1 (some public services and walking rotation), while mask and glove wearing remains mandatory.

2-34136-1-t.subevent: A woman pleaded with Insulate Britain protesters blocking the Blackwall Tunnel to let her through to see her mother, who she said was in hospital.
Activists sat on the northbound A102 at Blackwall Tunnel and three other major routes in London: Wandsworth Bridge, Hanger Lane, and Arnos Grove.
Furious motorists at Wandsworth Bridge dragged protesters out of the road, with one driver shouting that an ambulance was being blocked.
Insulate Britain founder Roger Hallam defended the protests, stating he would not have moved for the woman trying to get to the hospital.
Another Insulate Britain leader, Liam Norton, said the group would stop if the government made a meaningful statement, and defended blocking ambulances as necessary to highlight climate issues.
The Metropolitan Police arrested 38 people on suspicion of disrupting the highway and conspiracy to cause public nuisance in connection with the protests.
The Met Police stated that the protests were unreasonable and that they were acting quickly to minimize disruption.
Nine Insulate Britain activists admitted flouting a High Court injunction banning protests on the M25, which had been obtained by National Highways.

3-18013-3-t.subevent: The Chang'e-5 return capsule performed a ballistic skip reentry at 12:33 p.m. Eastern Dec. 16.
The capsule landed in the grasslands of Siziwang Banner at 12:59 p.m. and was located by recovery vehicles.
The samples will be delivered to a specially constructed laboratory in Beijing for preparation, analysis and storage.
The Chang'e-6 backup mission will be repurposed for a landing at the lunar South Pole or South Pole-Aitken Basin.
The Chang'e-5 orbiter performed a burn following separation of the return capsule to avoid reentering the atmosphere.
Chang'e-5 landed near Mons Rümker in Oceanus Procellarum on Dec. 1 and collected 0.5 kg of samples by drilling and scooping.

Chang'e-5 launched Nov. 23 and entered lunar orbit 112 hours later; after sampling, an ascent vehicle delivered the material into lunar orbit, and an automated rendezvous and docking transferred 2 kg into the return capsule.

0-4378-1-1.subevent: On October 21, 2016, Anthony Ferrante arrived at work and the internet went down across the US and parts of Europe due to the Dyn cyberattack.
Ferrante, a White House cybersecurity director, feared the attack was a dry run for interference in the upcoming presidential election.
Ferrante had a background in the FBI and was now running the National Security Council's Cyber Incident Response Desk, focusing on Russian election interference.
In summer 2016, the FBI discovered that Russian hackers had penetrated Illinois's voter database and targeted other states, scanning election websites in every state.
President Obama tasked Ferrante with creating a national cybersecurity preparedness plan for the election.
The Dyn attack was eventually mitigated by the company Dyn restoring their servers, but the perpetrator remains unknown.
On Election Day, Ferrante monitored the vote from the White House Situation Room; no major incidents occurred, but Russia had already interfered by hacking the DNC and spreading disinformation.
Obama imposed sanctions on Russia and expelled diplomats, but the Trump administration did not prioritize election security, and agencies achieved less than expected.
Experts described a hypothetical 2020 attack involving malware on voter registration databases and Trump potentially refusing to concede, a scenario that worries former official David Kris.

2-34957-1-1.subevent: Pope Francis blessed two large 'Voice of the Unborn' bells before the general audience at the Vatican on Oct. 27.
The bells are part of an initiative by the Polish Yes to Life foundation, and last year Pope Francis blessed a similar bell that traveled to nearly 30 cities in Poland.
Pope Francis stated that the bells are destined for Ecuador and Ukraine as a sign of commitment to defend human life from conception to natural death.
He entrusted to the prayers of the pilgrims every conceived child whose life is sacred and inviolable.
One bell will be given to the St. John Paul II Shrine in Lviv, Ukraine, and the other to the Diocese of Guayaquil in Ecuador.
The bells will travel to various events in those cities so people can ring them as an expression of pro-life beliefs.
The bells were cast in the workshop of Jan Felczyński in Przemyśl, each weighing over 2,000 pounds and nearly four feet in diameter.
The bells are decorated with a DNA chain, an ultrasound of an unborn child, and an image of the stone tables with the fifth commandment in Spanish and Ukrainian.
The bells also bear the words of Jeremiah 1:5 and a quote from St. John Paul II's encyclical Evangelium vitae.

0-4540-4-1.subevent: Japan colonized Korea from 1910 to 1945, forcing Koreans into labor and military brothels.
In 1965, South Korea normalized relations with Japan in exchange for loans and grants, which Tokyo considers a full settlement.
South Korea argues that the 1965 deal did not address individual reparations, leaving the issue unresolved.
In 2015, Japan apologized and pledged funds for 'comfort women' victims, but activists and President Moon Jae-in rejected the agreement.
In 2018, a South Korean court ordered Mitsubishi Heavy to compensate forced labor victims; the company refused and assets were seized.
The dispute sparked boycotts in South Korea and renewed tensions over disputed islands.
In August 2019, Japan removed South Korea's favored trade partner status and imposed export controls on electronics.
South Korea responded by ending a military intelligence-sharing pact with Japan, prompting Japanese protests and stock market declines.
In November 2019, South Korea reversed its decision and continued the intelligence-sharing pact.

0-4889-3-t.subevent: Local reports said suspected jihadists killed at least 19 people in attacks in northern Burkina Faso over the weekend.
Radio Omega reported that gunmen attacked the village of Pobe Mengao in the Sahel region, killing at least 16 people.
Assailants stole motorcycles and other vehicles and burned shops in Pobe Mengao.
The Burkina Faso News Agency reported that three people, including a teacher, were killed in Rounga in Lorum province on Friday and Saturday.
Extremists linked to al-Qaida and the Islamic State group have crossed from Mali into Burkina Faso in recent months, displacing hundreds of thousands of people.

19-28672-12-t.subevent: Saudi Arabia has asked Muslims planning to take part in the Hajj pilgrimage to delay booking amid uncertainty over the coronavirus pandemic.
Hajj Minister Mohammed Banten said the kingdom was concerned about the safety of pilgrims and urged people to 'wait before concluding contracts'.
Some two million people were expected to travel to Mecca and Medina this July and August for the annual gathering.
The lesser pilgrimage, the Umra, has already been suspended as a precaution to try to reduce the spread of the coronavirus.
People are also being prevented from entering Mecca and Medina, as well as the capital Riyadh, as the Saudi authorities attempt to contain an outbreak of Covid-19.
The outbreak of Covid-19 has infected at least 1,563 people and claimed 10 lives in the country.
Mr Banten told state TV that the kingdom is fully ready to serve pilgrims but is keen to protect the health of Muslims and citizens.

The minister added that the Hajj and health ministries had been inspecting hotels currently used to accommodate Umra pilgrims who had been told to self-isolate or been unable to return home, and that people who had purchased unused Umra visas would be refunded the cost.

3-18136-5-t.subevent: The Church of England announced on Tuesday it would suspend public worship to slow the spread of the coronavirus.
The Archbishops of Canterbury and York wrote a letter to clergy stating that church life would be less characterized by Sunday attendance and more by daily prayer and service.
PA Media reported that church weddings and funerals would continue.

0-4546-1-1.subevent: Three people died in Southern California wildfires: one civilian from cardiac arrest in the Saddleridge Fire and two found dead in the Sandalwood Fire.
The Saddleridge Fire ignited late Thursday in Sylmar, destroying or damaging 31 structures and burning over 7,900 acres, with 33% containment as of Saturday night.
California Governor Gavin Newsom and Los Angeles Mayor Eric Garcetti issued emergency declarations on Friday, and Newsom secured a FEMA grant.
Over 1,000 firefighters from multiple agencies battled the fire, which was fueled by strong Santa Ana winds and forced closures of freeways and evacuations in several communities.
276 minors were evacuated from a juvenile detention center in Sylmar to a facility 40 miles away, while Olive View Hospital was under shelter-in-place and an urgent care center was evacuated.
The Sandalwood Fire in Riverside County was 68% contained at about 1,000 acres, with 74 structures destroyed and an evacuation order in place at a mobile home park where two bodies were found.

Earlier in the week, PG&E began proactively shutting off power to 800,000 customers in Northern and Central California due to high wind concerns, and Southern California Edison cut power to over 21,000 customers but later reduced to 54.
SoCalGas tweeted that there were no indications of damage or leaks at the Aliso Canyon natural gas facility near Porter Ranch.

1-15033-1-1.subevent: Countries are shoveling huge sums of money at drug companies to aid development, clinical trials, and mass production of COVID-19 vaccines.
This financial activity overshadows coordinated global efforts.

6-18759-1-t.subevent: Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Nahyan buys a 50% stake in Beitar Jerusalem for $92 million over 10 years.
Sheikh Hamad says he is thrilled to be a partner.
The UAE and Bahrain sign an agreement to establish diplomatic relations with Israel at the White House.
Beitar Jerusalem's offices are set on fire after signing two Chechen Muslim footballers, and two La Familia members are charged with arson.
Moshe Hogeg launches an anti-racism campaign after buying the club and warns fans he will sue them for racist comments.
Hogeg signs the deal with Sheikh Hamad despite opposition from some supporters.
Hogeg says the move symbolizes a new light and leads to coexistence.
Sheikh Hamad says he is happy to take part in the change and refers to Jerusalem as the capital of Israel.

1-15313-3-t.subevent: A group of virus experts argued that the coronavirus pandemic almost certainly originated from an animal, probably at a wildlife market in China, and not from a laboratory leak, saying theories about a lab leak are based on coincidence, not hard evidence.
The experts, including leading coronavirus and virus genetics scientists, analyzed the evidence and published a pre-print review online.
They contended there is substantial scientific evidence supporting a zoonotic origin for SARS-CoV-2.

They stated there is no evidence that SARS-CoV-2 has a laboratory origin, that any early cases had connection to the Wuhan Institute of Virology, or that the institute possessed or worked on a progenitor of the virus.

They argued that the coincidence of first detection in Wuhan, which houses a major virology lab, is not surprising because Wuhan is a large city with animal markets and a major travel hub, and they said it is extremely unlikely that a lab accidentally leaked a natural virus.
Robert Garry noted that valuable evidence was lost when the animal markets in Wuhan were cleared and sanitized, and he wished the Chinese government would be more open about the wildlife trade.
The World Health Organization issued a report in March saying it was most likely the virus originated in an animal and passed to people, with a lab leak considered least likely.
The WHO investigation has focused on early cases at Wuhan's Huanan Seafood market, but the administration of President Joe Biden has been taking another look at the origins.

On Monday, another group of scientists in a letter to the Lancet called for careful and transparent collection of scientific information to understand the virus's spread, saying allegations and conjecture are not helpful.
